name: Zero-carb carnivore

card.summary: Animal foods only and no plants at all: popular online, supported mostly by self-reports, and classed as a fad diet by dietetic bodies.
card.note: Long-term safety has not been established; no large randomised trials exist.

quick.overview:
The zero-carb carnivore diet allows only animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and sometimes dairy, with no plant foods and no added carbohydrate. Trace carbohydrate from animal sources is treated as acceptable. Shawn Baker and the Petersons helped popularise it from about 2017 to 2019.

Believers report better weight, digestion, mood and skin. The published evidence is limited to a 2021 self-selected survey, case reports and small series.
quick.mechanism: With almost no carbohydrate the body relies on fat and protein for energy, usually in ketosis. Advocates argue that excluding plant compounds such as lectins and oxalates helps some people and that animal foods supply bioavailable nutrients such as heme iron, B12 and preformed vitamin A.
quick.risks: Reported or discussed risks include lack of fibre, possible shortfalls of vitamin C and other micronutrients, sharply raised LDL cholesterol in some people, constipation, gout and kidney strain. The British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify it as a fad diet.

lead: The carnivore diet, also called the zero-carb diet, is a high-protein, low-carbohydrate regimen in which adherents eat only animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs.[1] People in appearance communities use it to lose body fat and look leaner, and followers also report clearer skin and less bloating, which they credit to removing plant foods, sugar and processed food.[2][5]

The strict zero-carb version is described as the baseline, with no plants and no added carbohydrates, and trace carbohydrate from animal sources, generally under 5 grams a day, treated as acceptable.[2] Variants range from a beef, salt and water 'lion diet' to inclusive versions with fish, eggs and dairy, to the 'animal-based' diet of Paul Saladino that adds fruit, honey and raw dairy.[1][13] The modern movement grew from social media: orthopaedic surgeon Shawn Baker promoted the diet from 2017 to 2018 and in a 2019 book, Jordan Peterson and his daughter Mikhaila Peterson became prominent adherents of the lion diet, and the beef-only version later spread on TikTok.[1][2][11][14]

Research on the diet itself is limited to self-selected surveys, case reports and small series. A 2021 online survey of 2,029 adherents, summarised by Grokipedia, found that 95 percent reported feeling better overall, while a 2026 scoping review of nine human studies reported short-term weight loss, greater satiety and possible improvements in inflammatory or metabolic markers alongside nutrient shortfalls and raised LDL cholesterol, and judged the evidence very limited.[2][15] Professional dietetic bodies such as the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia regard it as a fad diet, according to Wikipedia.[1] Short- and medium-term trials of low-carbohydrate diets more generally have found more early weight loss than low-fat diets, an advantage reviews describe as fading over time.[3]

chain: Animal-only eating removes carbohydrate and most processed food
Appetite and calories often fall, and people report less bloating
Lower body fat and, by self-report, clearer skin
angle.text: Followers adopt it to cut body fat and to look leaner and less puffy, and some say their skin improves. These outcomes come from self-reported accounts rather than controlled trials.

paras: Zero-carb eating excludes all plant foods and relies on fat and protein for energy, usually through ketosis.[2] Followers eat beef, pork, poultry, fish and seafood, and some include eggs and dairy; fruits, vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds are left out.[1] Wikipedia notes that the diet is often compared with traditional Inuit eating, which differed in its high organ and seafood content, raw meat and gathered plant foods.[1]

Variants include stricter beef-only forms, inclusive versions with poultry, fish, eggs and low-lactose dairy, ketovore versions allowing about 10 grams of carbohydrate a day from low-carb plants, and the animal-based approach that permits fruit, honey and raw dairy.[1][2] A branch called carnivore traditionalism favours grass-fed beef and eggs from small farms, under the slogan 'It's not the cow, it's the how', in opposition to industrial livestock production.[1]

Bernard Moncriff's 1856 book The Philosophy of the Stomach promoted an exclusively animal diet, and he lived for a year on beef and milk; Arnaldo Cantani used animal-based diets for diabetic patients in the 1870s, and James H. Salisbury advocated lean beef and hot water in the 1880s.[1] Grokipedia cites John Rollo's 1797 diabetes treatment and reanalysed Inuit records suggesting roughly 10 percent of energy from carbohydrate.[2]

Explorer Vilhjalmur Stefansson and Karsten Anderson agreed to an observed study of living on meat alone for a year, with periodic examinations at Bellevue Hospital in New York, and results were published in 1929. The report concluded that prolonged meat-only living was possible without ill effects on the tests performed, that the diet was moderately high in protein and very high in fat, that lean meat alone was poorly tolerated, and that a mild state of ketosis resulted; it also called the diet expensive and not recommended for universal use. Wikipedia says the American Meat Institute funded the study, and Arctic physiologist Kare Rodahl later disputed that Stefansson's diet equalled the true Inuit diet, which included entrails and plant foods.[12]

Baker appeared on the Joe Rogan Experience in December 2017, Jordan Peterson in July 2018, and Baker published his book on the diet in 2019, which Grokipedia says drove popularity in the late 2010s alongside the Petersons' public testimony.[2]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and online communities
paras: Carnivore content spread through YouTube, podcasts, Instagram, TikTok and the r/carnivore subreddit, which Grokipedia says has thousands of members; by 2024 female 'meatfluencers' had broadened its appeal.[2] A study published in the Journal of Health, Population and Nutrition analysed one month of Instagram content from 19 carnivore creators with an average of about 158,000 followers and 1,169 posts; the posts focused heavily on health and disease, emphasised red meat and portrayed the diet positively, and some mixed in anti-institutional themes.[15]

A 2018 Hacker News thread discussed a news story on tech workers who adopted an all-meat diet to gain an edge on peers, with commenters raising ketosis, cognitive effects and fibre concerns.[5][6] Other threads there include a 90-day personal account and a discussion of mental health claims.[7][8]

Followers who use the diet for appearance describe faster fat loss and a leaner, less puffy face, and some report skin changes, which they link to dropping sugar and processed foods; these accounts are self-reported.[2][5]
Shawn Baker, an orthopaedic surgeon and powerlifter, is the best-known early advocate, credited with starting the 2018 wave through social media and his book.[1][2]

Mikhaila Peterson, born in 1992, began a carnivore diet in 2018 after a childhood of juvenile arthritis and hip and ankle replacements at 17; she followed the lion diet, which she described in an Instagram caption as 'Beef, salt, water and bourbon = cured.' She later hosted a podcast and briefly offered private consultations, and her blog drew criticism from commentators including a McGill University piece.[11] Jordan Peterson restricted his diet to meat and a few vegetables in 2016, eliminated vegetables by mid-2018, and ate beef, salt and water; nutrition experts quoted in his Wikipedia article warned of risks.[14]

Paul Saladino, a psychiatrist born in 1977, wrote The Carnivore Code in 2020, calling plants 'poison', then moved to an animal-based diet with fruit and honey, citing side effects of the strict version such as sleep problems, palpitations and lower testosterone. He co-owns the organ-supplement company Heart and Soil and has been criticised by science communicators such as Joseph Schwarcz.[13] Neurologist Steven Novella called the diet a fad in April 2023 and said its cost made it for 'select elites'.[1]

Advocates argue that humans evolved eating mostly animal foods, that plant compounds such as lectins and oxalates cause problems for some people, and that animal foods provide bioavailable nutrients such as heme iron, B12 and preformed vitamin A.[2] They also say that removing carbohydrate stabilises blood sugar and insulin, reduces appetite and aids weight loss, and that the diet works as an elimination diet for digestive, skin and autoimmune complaints.[2][11]

A 2024 nutrient analysis of four hypothetical Australian carnivore meal plans found they met reference values for riboflavin, niacin, phosphorus, zinc, B6, B12, vitamin A and selenium but fell short on thiamin, magnesium, calcium and vitamin C and sometimes iron, folate, iodine and potassium, with fibre far below recommendations.[15]

Advocates say the diet stabilises blood sugar and insulin, aids weight loss, eases autoimmune, digestive, skin and mood problems, and provides bioavailable nutrients.[2] In the 2021 survey, Grokipedia reports that 98 percent of respondents with diabetes or insulin resistance and 93 percent of those with overweight or obesity reported benefits, while adverse effects were reported by a small minority.[2]
A lab subset of that survey showed median LDL rising from 126 to 172 mg/dL, HDL from 58 to 68 and triglycerides falling from 83 to 68, according to Grokipedia, so lipid changes are mixed.[2]

Wikipedia lists the lack of fibre, vitamin deficiencies from excluding fruit and vegetables, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, higher risk of colon cancer and gout with high red-meat intake, and possible kidney impairment, and says nutrition scientists and professional bodies criticise it as extreme.[1]

A German observational study of 24 self-designed carnivore dieters found total cholesterol rising from a median of 224 to 305 mg/dL and LDL from 157 to 256 mg/dL, with the authors flagging the rise as a concern, while two pre-diabetic participants and six with high triglycerides saw those values fall.[15] The 2026 scoping review listed deficiencies in vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fibre, and did not recommend long-term adherence.[15] Grokipedia adds a documented scurvy case, LDL above 500 mg/dL in two patients that normalised when carbohydrate returned, and kidney-stone concerns, and describes a pilot microbiome study of one long-term follower finding normal diversity.[2] A 2025 Hacker News thread discusses a case report titled 'Yellowish Nodules on a Man Consuming a Carnivore Diet'.[10]
Saladino has said he left the strict version after sleep problems, palpitations and lower testosterone.[13] Critics also cite livestock emissions, while supporters cite regenerative grazing.[1][2]

No controlled trials of a long-term zero-carb carnivore diet have been published. Evidence consists of a 2021 survey of 2,029 adherents who had followed the diet for at least six months, a self-selected and self-reported sample, along with the German 24-person study, case reports and small series such as a 2024 series of 10 patients with inflammatory bowel disease reporting clinical remission.[2][15]

A 2025 review by R. D. Palmer of nearly 100 papers argued meat supports muscle growth and short-term nutrition but carries long-term adverse effects, recommending a shift toward white meat or plant protein for longevity.[15]

lore.intro: Carnivore advocates present the diet as a human-optimal elimination diet, and it is discussed on Hacker News and lifting forums.[2][5]

claims.claim: No plant foods are needed and plants can be harmful.
claims.believers: Advocates point to plant compounds like lectins and oxalates and to animal-heavy traditional diets such as the Inuit and Maasai.[2]
claims.experts: Dietetic bodies cite nutrient and fibre gaps; the claim about plant harms is described as largely anecdotal.[1][2]

claims.claim: Zero-carb carnivore reverses type 2 diabetes and aids weight loss.
claims.believers: Supporters cite stabilised blood sugar and case reports of remission.[2]
claims.experts: Short-term low-carb studies show weight loss, with the advantage fading in reviews at two years; the evidence for carnivore eating itself is limited to surveys and case reports.[2][3]

claims.claim: Ketosis from an all-meat diet sharpens thinking.
claims.believers: Commenters in the 2018 Hacker News discussion said the brain performs differently in ketosis and that a cognitive benefit may outweigh risks.[5]
claims.experts: Skeptics in the same thread noted links between red meat and health risks and bowel problems without vegetables; no controlled study of cognition on this diet was found.[5]

claims.claim: High LDL on carnivore is harmless.
claims.believers: Some advocates argue the LDL particles are benign.[2]
claims.experts: Mainstream guidance disagrees and treats raised LDL as a cardiovascular risk factor.[1][2]

claims.claim: The lion diet cures autoimmune disease
claims.believers: Mikhaila Peterson credits it with dramatic improvement of her juvenile arthritis and depression, and followers share similar accounts.[11]
claims.experts: Her blog was criticised as 'quackery' in coverage cited by Wikipedia, and no controlled trial has tested the lion diet.[11][2]

claims.claim: Plants are poison and meat-only eating is optimal
claims.believers: Saladino's 2020 book argued plants defend themselves with toxins and that animal foods are nutritionally superior.[13]
claims.experts: Schwarcz argues Saladino exaggerates risks and dismisses vegetables with anti-carcinogenic links; Saladino later moved to a version that includes fruit and honey.[13]

claims.claim: Meat-only eating gives a leaner, clearer look
claims.believers: Followers report fat loss and less bloating and puffiness within weeks, and some report clearer skin.[2][5]
claims.experts: Short-term low-carb diets lead to early weight loss, an advantage that fades in longer trials; no studies were found on skin outcomes.[3][15]

claims.claim: The diet is the natural human diet, as shown by the Inuit
claims.believers: Advocates cite Stefansson's 1928 meat-only year and Inuit traditions.[2][12]
claims.experts: Rodahl noted that Inuit also ate entrails and plants, and Wikipedia says the carnivore diet is often confused with Inuit cuisine.[1][12]
